en: The Questions of Milinda: The Section on the Refutation of the Puzzles (Meṇḍakapañha),
Chapter on What is Set Aside.
11. The Question on Non-violence and Restraint “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Practice non-violence in the world; you will be dear to me as if you were myself.’”
Furthermore, it has been said:
"One should restrain those who deserve restraint, and support those who deserve support.

But, venerable Nāgasena, what is called "restraint" consists of cutting off hands, cutting off feet, execution, imprisonment, torture, killing, and the disruption of one's lineage. This statement is not fitting for the Blessed One, nor does the Blessed One deserve to speak such words.
“Venerable Nāgasena, if it was said by the Blessed One:

‘Walk in harmlessness toward the world, and you shall be dear to me as myself,’ then that statement—‘One who deserves restraint should be restrained; one who deserves support should be supported’—is false.
If it was indeed spoken by the Tathāgata—”

“If [the Blessed One] said, ‘One should restrain those who deserve restraint, and encourage those who deserve encouragement,’ then the statement, ‘Walk in the world with harmlessness, and you will be dear to me as I am,’ must also be false.
This too is a dilemma from both sides that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Indeed, Great King, this was spoken by the Blessed One.”
"‘Practice non-violence in the world, and you will be dear to me as I am’—this has been said. And it was also said:
‘One who deserves restraint should be restrained; one who deserves encouragement should be encouraged.
‘Practice non-violence in the world, and you will be dear to me as I am’—this, O Great King, is the approval of all the Tathāgatas."
This is the instruction, this is the teaching of the Dhamma. For the Dhamma, Great King, is characterized by non-violence; it is a term for intrinsic nature.

But as for what the Tathāgata said, “One should restrain that which deserves restraint, and uplift that which deserves uplift”—this is a conventional expression. An agitated mind, Great King, should be restrained, and a sluggish mind should be uplifted.
An unwholesome mind is to be restrained; a wholesome mind is to be exerted.
Unwise attention is to be restrained; wise attention is to be exerted.
One who practices wrongly is to be restrained; one who practices rightly is to be exerted.
“The ignoble one must be restrained; the noble one must be encouraged. The thief must be restrained; the non-thief must be encouraged.
“Let it be so, venerable Nāgasena. Now you have returned to my domain; that which I asked has come before me.”
“But as for a thief, venerable Nāgasena, how should he be restrained when one is restraining him?

“A thief, great king, who is to be restrained should be restrained in this way: he should be rebuked when he deserves rebuke; he should be punished when he deserves punishment; he should be banished when he deserves banishment;
he should be bound when he deserves to be bound; he should be executed when he deserves execution. “But, venerable Nāgasena, is that execution of thieves approved by the Tathāgatas?”
“No indeed, Great King.
“But why, then, is it permitted by the Tathāgatas that a thief be punished?
“Great King, he who is executed is not executed by the permission of the Tathāgatas; rather, it is by his own doing.”

"He is being executed; moreover, he is being instructed according to the Dhamma. But, Great King, would it be possible for you to seize a man who has done nothing, who is innocent, and who is merely walking along the street, and have him executed?
"It would not be possible, venerable sir."
“For what reason, Great King?
“Because he is not the doer, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Great King, the thief is not killed by the Tathāgatas’ consent; he is killed by his own doing. But does the instructor incur any fault in this matter?”
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“In that case, great king, the instruction of the Tathāgatas is a correct instruction.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.”
The eleventh question: On Non-violence and Restraint.
